SESSION 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

From the course outline: Introduction to Microeconomics; product-manager decisions; scarcity, markets, models, positive/normative analysis and real versus nominal prices.

1.1 What is economics?

Economics studies how people and organisations make choices when resources are limited. We cannot have unlimited money, time, workers, machines or raw materials. Therefore, we must decide how to use what we have.

Simple example You have ₹500 for the week. You want food, travel, snacks and a movie. You cannot spend the same ₹500 on everything. Choosing one option means giving up another option. This is a trade-off.

1.2 What is microeconomics?

Microeconomics studies individual decision-makers and markets: consumers, firms, workers, products, prices and the interaction between buyers and sellers.

Microeconomics looks at…

Example

Consumer behaviour

Why a student chooses one phone brand over another.

Firm behaviour

How a food-delivery company decides its delivery fee.

Markets and prices

How demand and supply influence the price of milk.

Resource allocation

How a company uses workers, machines and money.

1.3 Why does a product manager need microeconomics?

The Session 1 slides ask what decisions product managers make and what information they need. A product manager may decide:

Product design: features, size and packaging.

Production: how much to produce and what capacity is required.

Market: where to sell and which customer segment to target.

Promotion: how to communicate the product.

Pricing: what price customers may accept and what price supports profitability.

Useful information includes what consumers want, segment size, profitability, production technology, capacity, resources, market structure, competitors, regulations, related markets, government policy and uncertainty.

Product example Before launching a low-cost student meal subscription, a product manager should estimate how many students need it, what they can pay, how much meals cost to prepare, what alternatives exist and whether supply can meet demand.

1.4 Circular-flow model

The circular-flow model shows how households and firms interact.

Who?

In the resource market

In the product market

Households

Supply resources such as labour and land.

Demand goods and services.

Firms

Demand resources to produce.

Supply goods and services.

Money flows in the opposite direction to real resources and products. Firms pay wages, rent and interest to households. Households use income to buy products, creating revenue for firms.

1.5 Markets and market structure

A market is the collection of buyers and sellers whose interaction determines the price of a product. Defining a market means deciding which buyers, sellers and products belong in it.

Market type

Basic meaning

Example from slides

Perfect competition

Many buyers and sellers; no single participant can influence market price.

Many agricultural markets.

Non-competitive market

One or more producers can influence price.

Electricity market; cartel example: OPEC.

Market structure affects how firms compete, how much control they have over price and what decisions they can make.

1.6 Theories, models and analysis

Term

Meaning

Example

Theory

A set of rules/assumptions used to explain observed behaviour.

Theory of consumer behaviour.

Model

A simplified or mathematical representation used to make predictions.

A demand equation predicting quantity at a price.

Positive analysis

Explains cause-and-effect; asks what is or what will happen.

What happens to demand if fuel tax rises?

Normative analysis

Asks what ought to happen; includes value judgements.

Should the government increase minimum wages?

1.7 Nominal price, real price and inflation

Nominal price is the current money price. Real price adjusts the nominal price for the overall price level, so prices from different years can be compared more fairly. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks the price of a basket of goods and services. Changes in CPI measure inflation.

Real price = (Base-year CPI ÷ Current-year CPI) × Current nominal price

Use the same CPI base as the lecture example. This converts a later price into base-year purchasing-power terms.

Lecture example: rice costs ₹7/kg in 2000–01 and ₹40/kg in 2019–20. CPI is 100 in 2000–01 and 800 in 2019–20. Real price at 2000–01 prices = (100/800) × 40 = ₹5/kg. The nominal price rose, but the inflation-adjusted price is ₹5 in base-year terms.

SESSION 2: Demand, Supply and Market Equilibrium

From the course outline: Demand and Supply; Market Equilibrium.

2.1 Demand

Demand means the quantity of a product consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices during a given period. Wanting a product is not enough: consumers also need the ability to pay.

The law of demand says that, other things remaining the same, when price rises, quantity demanded usually falls; when price falls, quantity demanded usually rises.

Price of a product

Typical quantity demanded

Higher price

Lower quantity demanded

Lower price

Higher quantity demanded

2.2 Demand curve and movement versus shift

A demand curve normally slopes downward. Price is on the vertical axis and quantity demanded is on the horizontal axis.

Change

What happens?

Example

Movement along demand curve

The product's own price changes; quantity demanded changes.

A pizza price falls from ₹200 to ₹150.

Demand curve shifts right

Demand increases at every price.

Income rises for a normal good; more consumers enter.

Demand curve shifts left

Demand decreases at every price.

A substitute becomes cheaper or consumer preference weakens.

Other demand factors include income, tastes/preferences, prices of related goods, expectations about future prices/income and number of buyers.

2.3 Related goods

Substitutes: goods that can replace each other. If the price of tea rises, some consumers may buy more coffee.

Complements: goods used together. If the price of printers rises sharply, demand for printer ink may fall.

2.4 Supply

Supply is the quantity producers are willing and able to sell at different prices during a given period. The law of supply says that, other things remaining the same, a higher price generally encourages producers to supply more.

A supply curve normally slopes upward. Higher prices can make production more profitable, encouraging firms to produce more.

Supply can shift because of input costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of sellers, expectations, weather or other production conditions.

2.5 Market equilibrium

Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. The price at this point is the equilibrium price, and the quantity is the equilibrium quantity.

At equilibrium: Qd = Qs

Situation

Meaning

Pressure on price

Qd > Qs

Shortage / excess demand

Buyers compete; price tends to rise.

Qs > Qd

Surplus / excess supply

Sellers compete; price tends to fall.

Qd = Qs

Equilibrium

No shortage or surplus at that price.

Remember Equilibrium is not simply a price that a company likes. It is the price at which the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell.

2.6 Worked equilibrium example

A vegetable fibre market has the following observations:

Price

Quantity demanded

Quantity supplied

₹1,200/kg

₹1,800/kg

Assume straight-line demand and supply curves between the observations. Demand falls by 12,000 kg when price rises by ₹600. Supply rises by 4,000 kg over the same price change.

Demand: Qd = 40,000 − 20P. Supply: Qs = 6.667P, where P is measured in rupees per kg. The supply equation fits both observations: at ₹1,200, supply is 8,000 kg; at ₹1,800, supply is 12,000 kg.

Equilibrium: 40,000 − 20P = 6.667P − 8,000

40,000 = 26.667P, so P ≈ ₹1,500/kg. Substituting into either equation: Q = 40,000 − 20(1,500) = 10,000 kg. Equilibrium is approximately ₹1,500 per kg and 10,000 kg.

SESSION 3: Elasticity of Demand and Supply

From the course outline: Price elasticity of demand and supply; factors influencing elasticity; revenue implications; income and cross-price elasticity.

3.1 Meaning of elasticity

Elasticity measures how strongly one variable responds when another variable changes. It is expressed as a percentage relationship, so it is useful for comparing products measured in different units.

Elasticity = % change in one variable ÷ % change in another variable

3.2 Price elasticity of demand (PED)

PED measures the percentage change in quantity demanded caused by a 1% change in price, other things remaining the same. Demand elasticity is usually negative because price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

PED = (% change in quantity demanded) ÷ (% change in price)

Point PED = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q)

For a straight-line demand function Q = a − bP, the slope ΔQ/ΔP is −b. The elasticity still depends on the point on the curve because P/Q changes.

3.3 Types of price elasticity

Type

Absolute value of PED

Meaning

Inelastic

Unit elastic

3.4 Arc elasticity

Arc elasticity measures responsiveness over a range between two price-quantity points. A common midpoint method is:

Arc PED = [(Q₂ − Q₁) / average Q] ÷ [(P₂ − P₁) / average P]

Average Q = (Q₁ + Q₂)/2 and average P = (P₁ + P₂)/2. The midpoint method avoids getting a different answer merely because you reverse the direction of the calculation.

3.5 Factors affecting price elasticity

Availability of close substitutes: more substitutes usually make demand more elastic.

Share of income spent: a product taking a larger share of income may have more elastic demand.

Durability: consumers may postpone buying durable products.

Possibility of postponing or repairing: if purchase can be delayed or product repaired, demand may respond more to price.

Time: consumers generally have more time to adjust in the long run.

3.6 Elasticity and total revenue

Total Revenue (TR) = Price (P) × Quantity sold (Q)

Demand type

If price decreases

TR unchanged

Elastic (|PED| > 1)

Managerial use Before reducing price, a product manager should ask whether the extra quantity sold will compensate for the lower price. If demand is inelastic, a price cut can reduce total revenue.

3.7 Income elasticity of demand

Income elasticity (YED) = % change in Qd ÷ % change in income

Sign

Interpretation

Positive

Normal good: demand increases when income increases.

Negative

Inferior good: demand decreases when income increases.

3.8 Cross-price elasticity of demand

Cross-price elasticity = % change in Qd of X ÷ % change in price of Y

Sign

Relationship

Positive

Substitutes: when price of Y rises, demand for X rises.

Negative

Complements: when price of Y rises, demand for X falls.

Near zero

Goods may be unrelated/independent.

3.9 Price elasticity of supply

PES = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price

Supply is usually more elastic in the long run because firms can expand capacity, hire workers, change production and adjust inputs. The lecture notes highlight durable goods as a special case: secondary supply through resale/recycling can make short-run supply relatively responsive.

3.10 Practice calculation

Price rises from ₹100 to ₹110 and quantity demanded falls from 200 to 180 units. Using the simple initial-value percentage method: %ΔQ = −20/200 = −10%; %ΔP = 10/100 = 10%; PED = −1. Demand is unit elastic at this comparison using the initial-value method.

SESSION 4: Consumer Preferences, Utility and Diminishing Marginal Utility

From the course outline: Consumer preferences, utility, indifference curves, marginal rate of substitution and the law of diminishing marginal utility.

4.1 Consumer behaviour

The lecture identifies three connected parts of consumer behaviour: preferences, budget constraints and the choices consumers make when income is limited.

4.2 Utility

Utility means the satisfaction or usefulness a consumer gets from consuming a good or combination of goods. A utility function assigns a number to a market basket. The number is useful for ranking choices; it does not need to measure happiness in a literal unit.

Example utility function: U(F,C) = F × C

If a basket contains 5 units of food and 5 units of clothing, U = 25. A basket with 10 units of food and 2.5 units of clothing also gives U = 25 in this example. These baskets are equally ranked by this utility function.

4.3 Consumer preference assumptions

Completeness: a consumer can compare/rank available market baskets.

Transitivity: if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A is preferred to C.

More is better: more of a good is preferred to less, assuming the good is desirable.

4.4 Indifference curves

An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction. An indifference map is a set of indifference curves.

Every point on one indifference curve gives the same utility.

A higher indifference curve represents a more preferred basket when more is better.

Indifference curves generally slope downward: to get more of one good while keeping satisfaction constant, the consumer must give up some of the other.

Indifference curves cannot intersect if preferences are consistent and transitive.

They are usually convex to the origin because the marginal rate of substitution diminishes.

4.5 Marginal rate of substitution (MRS)

MRS tells how much of one good a consumer is willing to give up to obtain one extra unit of another good while remaining equally satisfied. It is represented by the slope of the indifference curve.

MRS of food for clothing = amount of clothing given up ÷ extra food obtained

Diminishing MRS means that as a consumer gets more food and less clothing, the amount of clothing they are willing to give up for another unit of food usually decreases.

4.6 Perfect substitutes and perfect complements

Type

Indifference curve shape

Example

Perfect substitutes

Straight lines; constant MRS.

Two drinks a consumer considers interchangeable one-for-one.

Perfect complements

Right angles; goods are used together in fixed proportions.

Left shoe and right shoe.

4.7 Applying preferences to product design

The slides use car design as an application. A company may have to choose how much to spend on styling versus performance. Some customers value performance more, while others value styling more. Understanding which customer group is larger helps the company decide where to invest.

The solar-cooker case in the outline also points to a practical question: what do users value in a product, and which design choices make it more useful to them?

4.8 Marginal utility and diminishing marginal utility

Marginal utility (MU) is the extra satisfaction from consuming one additional unit. The law of diminishing marginal utility says that as more units of a good are consumed, the additional satisfaction from each extra unit eventually becomes smaller.

SESSION 5: Budget Constraints and Consumer Choice

From the course outline: Budget line, income and price changes, utility maximisation, corner solutions and equal marginal principle.

5.1 Budget constraint

Preferences tell us what a consumer likes. A budget constraint tells us what the consumer can afford. A consumer cannot buy every desired product because income is limited and goods have prices.

M = PₓQₓ + PᵧQᵧ

M is income, Pₓ and Pᵧ are the prices of two goods, and Qₓ and Qᵧ are the quantities purchased. The budget line shows combinations that use the entire budget.

5.2 Budget line example

Suppose monthly income is ₹80, price of food is ₹1 and price of clothing is ₹2. If all income is spent on food, the consumer can buy 80 units. If all income is spent on clothing, the consumer can buy 40 units.

5.4 Consumer choice / utility maximisation

A consumer chooses the most preferred basket they can afford. The best basket must be on the budget line (if more is better) and must be on the highest attainable indifference curve.

For an interior solution, the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line. At that point, their slopes are equal.

MRS = Pf/Pc

If MRS is not equal to the price ratio, the consumer can rearrange spending to become better off. The lecture states: if MRS is greater than the price ratio, increase food and reduce clothing until equality; if MRS is smaller, increase clothing and reduce food until equality.

5.5 Marginal utility per rupee / equal marginal principle

MUx/Px = MUy/Py

The consumer maximises utility when the marginal utility obtained from the last rupee spent on each good is equal. If one good gives more marginal utility per rupee, the consumer can shift spending toward it.

5.6 Corner solution

A corner solution occurs when a consumer chooses an extreme basket: all of one good and none of another. In that situation, the tangency condition MRS = price ratio does not necessarily hold.

5.7 Restricted versus unrestricted support

The lecture uses an education trust-fund example. If financial support must be spent only on education, it changes the consumer's available choices differently from unrestricted cash. An unrestricted gift can sometimes make the consumer better off because it allows spending across a wider set of goods.

SESSION 6: Individual Demand, Market Demand and Consumer Surplus

From the course outline: Individual and market demand, consumer surplus, network externalities and the link between consumer choice and demand.

6.1 Individual demand

An individual demand curve relates the price of a good to the quantity one consumer will buy, holding other factors constant. By changing the price and observing the consumer's chosen quantity, we can create a demand schedule and demand curve.

6.2 Income changes and Engel curves

When income rises and prices stay constant, the budget line shifts outward. For a normal good, quantity demanded rises and the demand curve shifts right. For an inferior good, quantity demanded falls as income rises.

6.3 Substitutes, complements and independent goods

Substitutes: a price rise in one good increases demand for the other. The lecture example is movie tickets and video rentals.

Complements: a price rise in one good reduces demand for the other. The lecture example is gasoline and motor oil.

Independent goods: a price change in one has no effect on demand for the other. The lecture example is chicken and airplane tickets.

6.5 Aggregating demand across markets

The slides show that total demand for a commodity can combine domestic demand and export demand. For wheat:

6.6 Consumer surplus

Consumer surplus is the difference between what a consumer is willing to pay and what the consumer actually pays. On a demand graph, it is the area below the demand curve and above the market price, up to the quantity purchased.

Example If you are willing to pay ₹1,000 for a product but buy it for ₹800, your consumer surplus on that purchase is ₹200.

6.7 Network externalities

For some products, one person's demand depends on how many other people use or buy the product. This is called a network externality.

Type

Meaning

Example / intuition

Positive network externality

Demand rises when more people use the product.

Bandwagon effect: people want a product because it is popular or fashionable.

Negative network externality

Demand falls when more people own/use the product.

Snob effect: people value a product because it is exclusive or rare.

A bandwagon effect can make demand shift further right as adoption grows. A snob effect can reduce the product's appeal as more people own it.

SESSION 7: Demand Estimation Methods

From the course outline: Demand estimation using regression, multiple factors, surveys, market experiments and database development.

7.1 What is demand estimation?

Demand estimation means using information and data to estimate how much customers may buy and how demand changes when factors such as price, income, advertising or competitor prices change.

7.2 Steps in demand estimation

Define the market: specify the product, geography, customer group and time period.

Identify segments: for example, students, families or business customers.

Identify demand drivers: price, income, technology, style, advertising, competitor prices and preferences.

Collect data: what customers say, what they currently buy and what they bought in the past.

Estimate the impact of each factor.

Validate the model and use it carefully for decisions.

7.3 Methods in the lecture slides

Method

How it works

Limitation / caution

Buyer-intention survey

Ask consumers how much they would buy at a given price.

People may lack information, interest or may not behave as they say.

Willingness-to-buy / pricing survey

Ask how likely a customer is to buy at different prices.

Stated willingness may differ from actual purchase.

Market experiment

Needs careful design and may cost money.

Test marketing

Launch in a limited market before wider launch.

Small test market may not represent all customers.

Pricing experiment

Change price in a controlled setting and observe sales.

Other changes must be controlled.

Regression analysis

Use historical data to estimate relationships between demand and drivers.

Results depend on data quality and correct model specification.

7.4 Regression basics

Regression estimates the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more explanatory variables. For demand, quantity demanded is often the dependent variable.

Simple linear demand: Q = a + bP

For a normal downward-sloping demand relationship, b is usually negative. A multiple regression model includes several factors:

Qx = a₀ + a₁Px + a₂N + a₃I + a₄Py + a₅T

Symbol

Meaning

Qx

Quantity demanded of product X

Px

Own price of product X

N

Number of buyers / population

I

Income

Py

Price of related product Y

T

Tastes, preferences or other factors

The coefficient for each variable estimates the change in Q associated with a one-unit change in that variable, holding the other included variables constant.

7.5 Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

OLS chooses the regression line that minimises the sum of squared vertical differences between actual observations and the line's predicted values. These differences are called residuals or errors.

Residual = Actual value − Predicted value

Squaring residuals prevents positive and negative errors from cancelling and gives larger errors more weight.

7.6 R-squared / goodness of fit

R-squared measures the proportion of variation in the dependent variable explained by the regression model, in the sample.

R² = 1 − (SSE / SST)

A higher R-squared means the model explains a larger share of the sample variation. It does not prove that the model is correct, that the relationship is causal or that forecasts will always be accurate.

7.7 Statistical significance

A coefficient estimate varies from sample to sample. Its standard error measures the uncertainty around the estimate. A t-statistic compares the estimate with its standard error.

t-statistic = Estimated coefficient ÷ Standard error

The slides refer to degrees of freedom n − k and comparing the calculated t-statistic with a critical value. A coefficient that is statistically significant provides evidence that its relationship is unlikely to be zero under the test assumptions.

SESSION 8: Production Decisions of a Company

From the course outline: Production function, short run and long run, marginal and average product, diminishing returns, two-input production, isoquants and returns to scale.

8.1 Production and inputs

Production is the process of transforming inputs into outputs. Inputs can include land, labour, capital and raw materials. Outputs are goods or services, such as cars, desks, books, ice cream or sugar.

8.2 Production function

Q = f(L, K)

A production function shows the maximum output a firm can produce from a given combination of inputs when it operates efficiently. L represents labour and K represents capital in the lecture's simplified model.

8.3 Short run and long run

Short run

Long run

At least one input is fixed; other inputs can vary.

All inputs can be changed.

Lecture simplification: labour varies, capital is fixed.

Both labour and capital can vary.

8.4 Average product and marginal product

Average Product of Labour (APL) = Q / L

Marginal Product of Labour (MPL) = ΔQ / ΔL

Average product is output per unit of labour. Marginal product is the additional output from one extra unit of labour, holding other inputs constant.

8.5 Law of diminishing marginal returns

When more of a variable input is used while other inputs are fixed, the extra output from each additional unit of that input will eventually decrease. For example, adding more workers to a small kitchen while keeping the same equipment and space may eventually create crowding.

Do not confuse Diminishing marginal returns does not mean total output immediately falls. Total output can continue to rise, but by smaller and smaller amounts.

8.6 Technology and productivity

The law of diminishing marginal returns assumes technology is constant. Better technology can shift the production function upward, allowing more output from the same inputs. The slides use this to explain why Malthus's prediction of mass hunger did not fully account for technological change.

8.7 Two variable inputs and isoquants

In the long run, a firm can combine different quantities of labour and capital to produce the same output. An isoquant shows all input combinations that produce the same level of output.

An isoquant is similar in purpose to an indifference curve: one describes equal output from input combinations; the other describes equal satisfaction from consumption combinations.

8.8 Marginal rate of technical substitution (MRTS)

MRTS measures how much of one input (such as capital) can be reduced when one extra unit of another input (such as labour) is used, while keeping output constant.

MRTS of labour for capital = MPL / MPK = −ΔK/ΔL

The slope of the isoquant is negative. The ratio of marginal products gives the absolute trade-off between inputs along the isoquant.

8.9 Perfect substitutes and complements in production

Perfect substitutes: one input can replace another at a constant rate; isoquants are straight lines.

Perfect complements: inputs must be used together in fixed proportions; isoquants are right angles.

8.10 Returns to scale

Returns to scale describe what happens to output when all inputs are increased by the same proportion.

Type

If all inputs double…

Increasing returns to scale

Output more than doubles.

Constant returns to scale

Output exactly doubles.

Decreasing returns to scale

Output less than doubles.

Do not confuse returns to scale with diminishing marginal returns. Diminishing marginal returns changes one input while other inputs are fixed. Returns to scale changes all inputs proportionately.

SESSION 9: Cost of Production

From the course outline: Fixed, variable, total, average and marginal costs; opportunity and sunk costs; short-run and long-run costs; economies of scale and scope; learning curve.

9.1 Why do firms study costs?

A firm needs to understand how production choices affect costs. Cost information helps managers choose how much to produce, which inputs to use, whether to expand and how to price products.

9.2 Fixed, variable and total cost

Cost

Meaning

Example

Fixed cost (FC)

Does not change with output in the short run.

Rent for a factory or fixed equipment lease.

Variable cost (VC)

Changes as output changes.

Raw materials, packaging and production labour.

Total cost (TC)

Fixed cost plus variable cost.

All fixed and variable production costs.

TC = FC + VC

Whether a cost is fixed or variable depends on the time horizon. A factory lease may be fixed in the short run, but the firm may change its premises in the long run.

9.3 Average costs

Average Fixed Cost (AFC) = FC / Q

Average Variable Cost (AVC) = VC / Q

Average Total Cost (ATC) = TC / Q = AFC + AVC

Average cost means cost per unit. As output rises, AFC usually falls because the same fixed cost is spread across more units.

9.4 Marginal cost

Marginal Cost (MC) = ΔTC / ΔQ

Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one additional unit. Since fixed cost does not change when output changes in the short run, marginal cost is also the change in variable cost divided by the change in output.

9.5 Opportunity cost and sunk cost

Concept

Meaning

Decision rule

Opportunity cost

Value of the best alternative given up when a resource is used.

Include it in economic decision-making.

Sunk cost

Past expenditure that has been made and cannot be recovered.

Do not let it determine a future decision.

Example from the slides: a firm owns its building and pays no rent. The economic cost of using the building is not zero because it could have rented the building out. The rent it gives up is an opportunity cost.

A non-refundable advance already paid for a building option is a sunk cost. If a better building becomes available, the firm should compare future costs and benefits rather than buy the first building merely because it has already paid the advance.

9.6 Costs in the short run

The lecture links marginal cost to marginal product of labour. If each extra worker adds a lot of output, the cost of producing an extra unit can be low. If each extra worker adds little output, marginal cost can be high.

Relationship Increasing marginal product of labour tends to reduce marginal cost. Decreasing marginal product of labour tends to increase marginal cost, assuming the wage rate is fixed.

9.7 Long-run cost and opportunity cost of capital

In the long run, firms can change capital and labour. The economic cost of capital includes depreciation and the return that could have been earned by investing the money elsewhere.

User cost of capital = Economic depreciation + (Interest rate × Value of capital)

The slides give an airplane example: purchase price $150 million, useful life 30 years, annual economic depreciation $5 million and interest rate 10%. In year 1, user cost is $5m + 10% × $150m = $20m.

9.8 Isocost line and cost-minimising input choice

An isocost line shows combinations of labour and capital that have the same total cost.

C = wL + rK

w is the wage rate, r is the price/rental rate of capital, L is labour and K is capital.

K = C/r − (w/r)L

The slope is −w/r. Combining an isocost line with an isoquant helps a firm find the lowest-cost input combination for a given output.

9.9 Short run versus long run costs

In the short run, some inputs are fixed, so the firm may not be able to produce at the lowest possible cost. In the long run, the firm can adjust plant size and capital, potentially lowering average cost for a given output.

9.10 Economies of scale, scope and learning curve

Concept

Meaning

Example

Economies of scale

Average cost falls as the scale/volume of production increases.

A larger factory spreads fixed costs and allows specialisation.

Diseconomies of scale

Average cost rises when the firm becomes too large or difficult to manage.

Coordination and management complexity.

Economies of scope

Producing two or more products together costs less than producing them separately.

A delivery network used for multiple product categories.

Learning curve

Unit cost falls as cumulative experience or output increases.

Workers become faster and processes improve with practice.

9.11 Estimating cost

The cost deck includes a cubic cost function example:

TC = 200 + 5Q − 0.04Q² + 0.001Q³

From a total cost function, fixed cost is the part that does not depend on Q. Variable cost is the part that changes with Q. Average cost is TC/Q, and marginal cost is the derivative of TC with respect to Q.

For the example: FC = 200; VC = 5Q − 0.04Q² + 0.001Q³

MC = dTC/dQ = 5 − 0.08Q + 0.003Q²

SESSION 10: Firm’s Decision in a Competitive Market

From the course outline: Profit maximisation, price-taking firms, marginal revenue and marginal cost, short-run output and shutdown, firm and industry supply, long-run equilibrium.

10.1 Firm objective and profit

The lecture assumes that a firm's objective is to maximise profit.

Profit (π) = Total Revenue (TR) − Total Cost (TC)

TR = P × Q

Total cost includes fixed and variable costs and, in economic analysis, opportunity costs.

10.2 Perfectly competitive market

A competitive market is one in which no single firm can influence the market price. A firm in this market is a price taker: it accepts the market price.

Many buyers and sellers.

Firms sell a homogeneous/standardised product.

Individual firms cannot influence the market price.

The lecture's competitive-market discussion includes free entry and exit.

10.3 Revenue for a competitive firm

Because the firm is a price taker, it can sell additional units at the market price, within the model.

Average Revenue (AR) = TR/Q = P

Marginal Revenue (MR) = ΔTR/ΔQ = P

Key result For a perfectly competitive firm: P = AR = MR. The firm's demand curve is a horizontal line at the market price.

10.4 Profit maximisation rule

Choose output where MR = MC, provided producing is better than shutting down.

If MR is greater than MC, producing one more unit adds more revenue than cost, so increasing output raises profit. If MC is greater than MR, the extra unit costs more than it earns, so reducing output raises profit. The profit-maximising point is where MR and MC meet on the relevant rising part of MC.

10.5 Short-run decisions

In the short run, at least one input is fixed. A firm can make a profit, incur a loss and still choose to produce if revenue covers variable costs and contributes something toward fixed costs.

Condition

Decision intuition

P > ATC

Firm earns positive economic profit.

P = ATC

Firm earns zero economic profit (normal return included in economic cost).

AVC < P < ATC

Firm incurs a loss but may continue producing because it covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.

P < AVC

Firm should shut down in the short run under the standard rule because revenue does not cover variable cost.

Short-run shutdown rule: produce if P ≥ minimum AVC; shut down if P < minimum AVC.

10.6 Short-run supply curve

The firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of its marginal cost curve above the minimum point of average variable cost. It shows how much the firm will produce at different market prices.

10.7 Market / industry supply

The short-run market supply curve is obtained by adding the quantities supplied by all firms horizontally at each price. When price rises, firms generally expand output along their supply curves.

10.8 Long-run competitive equilibrium

In the long run, firms can enter or leave the industry and adjust all inputs. If firms earn positive economic profits, new firms have an incentive to enter. Entry increases industry supply and puts downward pressure on price and profit. If firms incur economic losses, some firms may exit, reducing supply and putting upward pressure on price.

In the standard long-run competitive equilibrium described in the lecture, firms maximise profit and earn zero economic profit. Zero economic profit does not mean the owner receives no return; normal opportunity costs are included in economic cost.

10.9 Industry long-run supply

The shape of the industry's long-run supply curve depends on how industry expansion affects the prices firms pay for inputs. If input prices remain unchanged, industry supply may be relatively flat; if input prices rise, it may slope upward; if input prices fall, it may slope downward. The exact case depends on the industry.

Worked numerical example

Suppose a competitive firm faces market price P = ₹100 and has marginal cost MC = 0.002Q. Under competition, MR = P.

MR = MC → 100 = 0.002Q → Q = 50,000 units

This is the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, subject to the shutdown condition and the relevant cost curves.

Practice Questions with Answers

1. What is the difference between microeconomics and macroeconomics?

Answer: Microeconomics studies individual consumers, firms and markets. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, such as inflation, unemployment and national income.

2. What happens when market price is below equilibrium?

Answer: Quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied, creating a shortage. This creates upward pressure on price.

3. A product's price rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 20%. Find PED.

Answer: PED = −20% ÷ 10% = −2. Absolute elasticity is 2, so demand is elastic.

4. If income rises and demand for a product falls, what type of good is it?

Answer: An inferior good. Its income elasticity is negative.

5. What does MRS = Px/Py mean?

Answer: At an interior consumer optimum, the consumer's willingness to trade one good for another equals the market price trade-off.

6. What is the difference between individual and market demand?

Answer: Individual demand is for one consumer. Market demand is the horizontal sum of all individual quantities demanded at each price.

7. A regression model has R² = 0.80. What does it mean?

Answer: The model explains 80% of the variation in the dependent variable in the sample. It does not prove causation or guarantee accurate predictions.

8. If 4 workers produce 80 units, what is average product of labour?

Answer: APL = Q/L = 80/4 = 20 units per worker.

9. Total cost rises from ₹500 to ₹560 when output rises from 10 to 12 units. Find marginal cost per additional unit over this range.

Answer: MC = ΔTC/ΔQ = (560−500)/(12−10) = 60/2 = ₹30 per unit.

10. A firm has FC ₹100, VC ₹300 and output 20 units. Find TC and ATC.

Answer: TC = 100 + 300 = ₹400. ATC = 400/20 = ₹20 per unit.

11. Why is rent foregone on an owned building an opportunity cost?

Answer: Because the firm gives up the rental income it could have earned by using the building itself.

12. A competitive firm has price ₹50 and MC reaches ₹50 at 100 units. What output satisfies the MR=MC rule?

Answer: MR = P = ₹50. The candidate profit-maximising output is 100 units, provided the firm should operate rather than shut down.

13. Explain the difference between economies of scale and economies of scope.

Answer: Scale means average cost falls as volume of one product rises. Scope means joint production of different products costs less than producing them separately.

14. Why might a firm continue producing while making a short-run loss?

Answer: If price covers average variable cost, the firm can cover variable costs and contribute something toward fixed costs. Shutting down would still leave fixed costs to pay.

15. What is the bandwagon effect?

Answer: A positive network externality in which people want a product partly because many others own or use it.

SESSION 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

From the course outline: Introduction to Microeconomics; product-manager decisions; scarcity, markets, models, positive/normative analysis and real versus nominal prices.

1.1 What is economics?

Economics studies how people and organisations make choices when resources are limited. We cannot have unlimited money, time, workers, machines or raw materials. Therefore, we must decide how to use what we have.

pages.title: Section 2
pages.text:
Simple example You have ₹500 for the week. You want food, travel, snacks and a movie. You cannot spend the same ₹500 on everything. Choosing one option means giving up another option. This is a trade-off.

1.2 What is microeconomics?

Microeconomics studies individual decision-makers and markets: consumers, firms, workers, products, prices and the interaction between buyers and sellers.

Microeconomics looks at…

Example

Consumer behaviour

Why a student chooses one phone brand over another.

Firm behaviour

How a food-delivery company decides its delivery fee.

Markets and prices

How demand and supply influence the price of milk.

Resource allocation

How a company uses workers, machines and money.

1.3 Why does a product manager need microeconomics?

The Session 1 slides ask what decisions product managers make and what information they need. A product manager may decide:

Product design: features, size and packaging.

Production: how much to produce and what capacity is required.

Market: where to sell and which customer segment to target.

Promotion: how to communicate the product.

Pricing: what price customers may accept and what price supports profitability.

Useful information includes what consumers want, segment size, profitability, production technology, capacity, resources, market structure, competitors, regulations, related markets, government policy and uncertainty.

Product example Before launching a low-cost student meal subscription, a product manager should estimate how many students need it, what they can pay, how much meals cost to prepare, what alternatives exist and whether supply can meet demand.

1.4 Circular-flow model

The circular-flow model shows how households and firms interact.

Who?

In the resource market

In the product market

Households

Supply resources such as labour and land.

Demand goods and services.

Firms

Demand resources to produce.

Supply goods and services.

pages.title: Section 3
pages.text:
Money flows in the opposite direction to real resources and products. Firms pay wages, rent and interest to households. Households use income to buy products, creating revenue for firms.

1.5 Markets and market structure

A market is the collection of buyers and sellers whose interaction determines the price of a product. Defining a market means deciding which buyers, sellers and products belong in it.

Market type

Basic meaning

Example from slides

Perfect competition

Many buyers and sellers; no single participant can influence market price.

Many agricultural markets.

Non-competitive market

One or more producers can influence price.

Electricity market; cartel example: OPEC.

Market structure affects how firms compete, how much control they have over price and what decisions they can make.

1.6 Theories, models and analysis

Term

Meaning

Example

Theory

A set of rules/assumptions used to explain observed behaviour.

Theory of consumer behaviour.

Model

A simplified or mathematical representation used to make predictions.

A demand equation predicting quantity at a price.

Positive analysis

Explains cause-and-effect; asks what is or what will happen.

What happens to demand if fuel tax rises?

Normative analysis

Asks what ought to happen; includes value judgements.

Should the government increase minimum wages?

1.7 Nominal price, real price and inflation

Nominal price is the current money price. Real price adjusts the nominal price for the overall price level, so prices from different years can be compared more fairly. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks the price of a basket of goods and services. Changes in CPI measure inflation.

Real price = (Base-year CPI ÷ Current-year CPI) × Current nominal price

Use the same CPI base as the lecture example. This converts a later price into base-year purchasing-power terms.

pages.title: Section 4
pages.text:
Lecture example: rice costs ₹7/kg in 2000–01 and ₹40/kg in 2019–20. CPI is 100 in 2000–01 and 800 in 2019–20. Real price at 2000–01 prices = (100/800) × 40 = ₹5/kg. The nominal price rose, but the inflation-adjusted price is ₹5 in base-year terms.

SESSION 2: Demand, Supply and Market Equilibrium

From the course outline: Demand and Supply; Market Equilibrium.

2.1 Demand

Demand means the quantity of a product consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices during a given period. Wanting a product is not enough: consumers also need the ability to pay.

The law of demand says that, other things remaining the same, when price rises, quantity demanded usually falls; when price falls, quantity demanded usually rises.

Price of a product

Typical quantity demanded

Higher price

Lower quantity demanded

Lower price

Higher quantity demanded

2.2 Demand curve and movement versus shift

A demand curve normally slopes downward. Price is on the vertical axis and quantity demanded is on the horizontal axis.

Change

What happens?

Example

Movement along demand curve

The product's own price changes; quantity demanded changes.

A pizza price falls from ₹200 to ₹150.

Demand curve shifts right

Demand increases at every price.

Income rises for a normal good; more consumers enter.

Demand curve shifts left

Demand decreases at every price.

A substitute becomes cheaper or consumer preference weakens.

Other demand factors include income, tastes/preferences, prices of related goods, expectations about future prices/income and number of buyers.

2.3 Related goods

pages.title: Section 5
pages.text:
Substitutes: goods that can replace each other. If the price of tea rises, some consumers may buy more coffee.

Complements: goods used together. If the price of printers rises sharply, demand for printer ink may fall.

2.4 Supply

Supply is the quantity producers are willing and able to sell at different prices during a given period. The law of supply says that, other things remaining the same, a higher price generally encourages producers to supply more.

A supply curve normally slopes upward. Higher prices can make production more profitable, encouraging firms to produce more.

Supply can shift because of input costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of sellers, expectations, weather or other production conditions.

2.5 Market equilibrium

Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. The price at this point is the equilibrium price, and the quantity is the equilibrium quantity.

At equilibrium: Qd = Qs

Situation

Meaning

Pressure on price

Qd > Qs

Shortage / excess demand

Buyers compete; price tends to rise.

Qs > Qd

Surplus / excess supply

Sellers compete; price tends to fall.

Qd = Qs

Equilibrium

No shortage or surplus at that price.

Remember Equilibrium is not simply a price that a company likes. It is the price at which the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell.

2.6 Worked equilibrium example

A vegetable fibre market has the following observations:

Price

Quantity demanded

Quantity supplied

₹1,200/kg

16,000 kg

8,000 kg

₹1,800/kg

4,000 kg

12,000 kg

Assume straight-line demand and supply curves between the observations. Demand falls by 12,000 kg when price rises by ₹600. Supply rises by 4,000 kg over the same price change.

Demand: Qd = 40,000 − 20P. Supply: Qs = 6.667P, where P is measured in rupees per kg. The supply equation fits both observations: at ₹1,200, supply is 8,000 kg; at ₹1,800, supply is 12,000 kg.

Equilibrium: 40,000 − 20P = 6.667P − 8,000

pages.title: Section 6
pages.text:
40,000 = 26.667P, so P ≈ ₹1,500/kg. Substituting into either equation: Q = 40,000 − 20(1,500) = 10,000 kg. Equilibrium is approximately ₹1,500 per kg and 10,000 kg.

SESSION 3: Elasticity of Demand and Supply

From the course outline: Price elasticity of demand and supply; factors influencing elasticity; revenue implications; income and cross-price elasticity.

3.1 Meaning of elasticity

Elasticity measures how strongly one variable responds when another variable changes. It is expressed as a percentage relationship, so it is useful for comparing products measured in different units.

Elasticity = % change in one variable ÷ % change in another variable

3.2 Price elasticity of demand (PED)

PED measures the percentage change in quantity demanded caused by a 1% change in price, other things remaining the same. Demand elasticity is usually negative because price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

PED = (% change in quantity demanded) ÷ (% change in price)

Point PED = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q)

For a straight-line demand function Q = a − bP, the slope ΔQ/ΔP is −b. The elasticity still depends on the point on the curve because P/Q changes.

3.3 Types of price elasticity

Type

Absolute value of PED

Meaning

Perfectly inelastic

0

Quantity does not change when price changes.

Inelastic

Between 0 and 1

Quantity changes by a smaller percentage than price.

Unit elastic

1

Quantity changes by the same percentage as price.

Elastic

Greater than 1

Quantity changes by a larger percentage than price.

Perfectly elastic

Infinite

Consumers buy at one price; at a higher price, quantity demanded falls to zero.

3.4 Arc elasticity

Arc elasticity measures responsiveness over a range between two price-quantity points. A common midpoint method is:

pages.title: Section 7
pages.text:
Arc PED = [(Q₂ − Q₁) / average Q] ÷ [(P₂ − P₁) / average P]

Average Q = (Q₁ + Q₂)/2 and average P = (P₁ + P₂)/2. The midpoint method avoids getting a different answer merely because you reverse the direction of the calculation.

3.5 Factors affecting price elasticity

Availability of close substitutes: more substitutes usually make demand more elastic.

Share of income spent: a product taking a larger share of income may have more elastic demand.

Durability: consumers may postpone buying durable products.

Possibility of postponing or repairing: if purchase can be delayed or product repaired, demand may respond more to price.

Time: consumers generally have more time to adjust in the long run.

Total Revenue (TR) = Price (P) × Quantity sold (Q)

Demand type

If price increases

If price decreases

Inelastic (|PED| < 1)

TR increases

TR decreases

Unit elastic (|PED| = 1)

TR unchanged

TR unchanged

Elastic (|PED| > 1)

SESSION 4: Consumer Preferences, Utility and Diminishing Marginal Utility

From the course outline: Consumer preferences, utility, indifference curves, marginal rate of substitution and the law of diminishing marginal utility.

4.1 Consumer behaviour

The lecture identifies three connected parts of consumer behaviour: preferences, budget constraints and the choices consumers make when income is limited.

4.2 Utility

Utility means the satisfaction or usefulness a consumer gets from consuming a good or combination of goods. A utility function assigns a number to a market basket. The number is useful for ranking choices; it does not need to measure happiness in a literal unit.

Example utility function: U(F,C) = F × C

If a basket contains 5 units of food and 5 units of clothing, U = 25. A basket with 10 units of food and 2.5 units of clothing also gives U = 25 in this example. These baskets are equally ranked by this utility function.

4.3 Consumer preference assumptions

Completeness: a consumer can compare/rank available market baskets.

Transitivity: if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A is preferred to C.

pages.title: Section 9
pages.text:
More is better: more of a good is preferred to less, assuming the good is desirable.

4.4 Indifference curves

An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction. An indifference map is a set of indifference curves.

Every point on one indifference curve gives the same utility.

A higher indifference curve represents a more preferred basket when more is better.

Indifference curves generally slope downward: to get more of one good while keeping satisfaction constant, the consumer must give up some of the other.

Indifference curves cannot intersect if preferences are consistent and transitive.

They are usually convex to the origin because the marginal rate of substitution diminishes.

4.5 Marginal rate of substitution (MRS)

MRS tells how much of one good a consumer is willing to give up to obtain one extra unit of another good while remaining equally satisfied. It is represented by the slope of the indifference curve.

MRS of food for clothing = amount of clothing given up ÷ extra food obtained

Diminishing MRS means that as a consumer gets more food and less clothing, the amount of clothing they are willing to give up for another unit of food usually decreases.

4.6 Perfect substitutes and perfect complements

The slides use car design as an application. A company may have to choose how much to spend on styling versus performance. Some customers value performance more, while others value styling more. Understanding which customer group is larger helps the company decide where to invest.

A consumer chooses the most preferred basket they can afford. The best basket must be on the budget line (if more is better) and must be on the highest attainable indifference curve.

The consumer maximises utility when the marginal utility obtained from the last rupee spent on each good is equal. If one good gives more marginal utility per rupee, the consumer can shift spending toward it.

A corner solution occurs when a consumer chooses an extreme basket: all of one good and none of another. In that situation, the tangency condition MRS = price ratio does not necessarily hold.

SESSION 7: Demand Estimation Methods

From the course outline: Demand estimation using regression, multiple factors, surveys, market experiments and database development.

7.1 What is demand estimation?

Demand estimation means using information and data to estimate how much customers may buy and how demand changes when factors such as price, income, advertising or competitor prices change.

7.2 Steps in demand estimation

Define the market: specify the product, geography, customer group and time period.

Identify segments: for example, students, families or business customers.

Identify demand drivers: price, income, technology, style, advertising, competitor prices and preferences.

Collect data: what customers say, what they currently buy and what they bought in the past.

Estimate the impact of each factor.

Validate the model and use it carefully for decisions.

7.4 Regression basics

Regression estimates the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more explanatory variables. For demand, quantity demanded is often the dependent variable.

Simple linear demand: Q = a + bP

For a normal downward-sloping demand relationship, b is usually negative. A multiple regression model includes several factors:

Qx = a₀ + a₁Px + a₂N + a₃I + a₄Py + a₅T

The coefficient for each variable estimates the change in Q associated with a one-unit change in that variable, holding the other included variables constant.

7.5 Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

OLS chooses the regression line that minimises the sum of squared vertical differences between actual observations and the line's predicted values. These differences are called residuals or errors.

Residual = Actual value − Predicted value

Squaring residuals prevents positive and negative errors from cancelling and gives larger errors more weight.

7.6 R-squared / goodness of fit

R-squared measures the proportion of variation in the dependent variable explained by the regression model, in the sample.

R² = 1 − (SSE / SST)

A higher R-squared means the model explains a larger share of the sample variation. It does not prove that the model is correct, that the relationship is causal or that forecasts will always be accurate.

7.7 Statistical significance

A coefficient estimate varies from sample to sample. Its standard error measures the uncertainty around the estimate. A t-statistic compares the estimate with its standard error.

t-statistic = Estimated coefficient ÷ Standard error

The slides refer to degrees of freedom n − k and comparing the calculated t-statistic with a critical value. A coefficient that is statistically significant provides evidence that its relationship is unlikely to be zero under the test assumptions.

SESSION 8: Production Decisions of a Company

From the course outline: Production function, short run and long run, marginal and average product, diminishing returns, two-input production, isoquants and returns to scale.

8.1 Production and inputs

pages.title: Section 17
pages.text:
Production is the process of transforming inputs into outputs. Inputs can include land, labour, capital and raw materials. Outputs are goods or services, such as cars, desks, books, ice cream or sugar.

8.2 Production function

Q = f(L, K)

A production function shows the maximum output a firm can produce from a given combination of inputs when it operates efficiently. L represents labour and K represents capital in the lecture's simplified model.

8.3 Short run and long run

Short run

Long run

At least one input is fixed; other inputs can vary.

All inputs can be changed.

Lecture simplification: labour varies, capital is fixed.

Both labour and capital can vary.

8.4 Average product and marginal product

Average Product of Labour (APL) = Q / L

Marginal Product of Labour (MPL) = ΔQ / ΔL

Average product is output per unit of labour. Marginal product is the additional output from one extra unit of labour, holding other inputs constant.

8.5 Law of diminishing marginal returns

When more of a variable input is used while other inputs are fixed, the extra output from each additional unit of that input will eventually decrease. For example, adding more workers to a small kitchen while keeping the same equipment and space may eventually create crowding.

Do not confuse Diminishing marginal returns does not mean total output immediately falls. Total output can continue to rise, but by smaller and smaller amounts.

8.6 Technology and productivity

The law of diminishing marginal returns assumes technology is constant. Better technology can shift the production function upward, allowing more output from the same inputs. The slides use this to explain why Malthus's prediction of mass hunger did not fully account for technological change.

8.7 Two variable inputs and isoquants

In the long run, a firm can combine different quantities of labour and capital to produce the same output. An isoquant shows all input combinations that produce the same level of output.

pages.title: Section 18
pages.text:
An isoquant is similar in purpose to an indifference curve: one describes equal output from input combinations; the other describes equal satisfaction from consumption combinations.

8.8 Marginal rate of technical substitution (MRTS)

MRTS measures how much of one input (such as capital) can be reduced when one extra unit of another input (such as labour) is used, while keeping output constant.

MRTS of labour for capital = MPL / MPK = −ΔK/ΔL

The slope of the isoquant is negative. The ratio of marginal products gives the absolute trade-off between inputs along the isoquant.

8.9 Perfect substitutes and complements in production

Perfect substitutes: one input can replace another at a constant rate; isoquants are straight lines.

Perfect complements: inputs must be used together in fixed proportions; isoquants are right angles.

8.10 Returns to scale

Returns to scale describe what happens to output when all inputs are increased by the same proportion.

Type

If all inputs double…

Increasing returns to scale

Output more than doubles.

Constant returns to scale

Output exactly doubles.

Decreasing returns to scale

Output less than doubles.

Do not confuse returns to scale with diminishing marginal returns. Diminishing marginal returns changes one input while other inputs are fixed. Returns to scale changes all inputs proportionately.

SESSION 9: Cost of Production

From the course outline: Fixed, variable, total, average and marginal costs; opportunity and sunk costs; short-run and long-run costs; economies of scale and scope; learning curve.

9.1 Why do firms study costs?

pages.title: Section 19
pages.text:
A firm needs to understand how production choices affect costs. Cost information helps managers choose how much to produce, which inputs to use, whether to expand and how to price products.

9.2 Fixed, variable and total cost

Cost

Meaning

Example

Fixed cost (FC)

Does not change with output in the short run.

Rent for a factory or fixed equipment lease.

Variable cost (VC)

Changes as output changes.

Raw materials, packaging and production labour.

Total cost (TC)

Fixed cost plus variable cost.

All fixed and variable production costs.

TC = FC + VC

Whether a cost is fixed or variable depends on the time horizon. A factory lease may be fixed in the short run, but the firm may change its premises in the long run.

9.3 Average costs

Average Fixed Cost (AFC) = FC / Q

Average Variable Cost (AVC) = VC / Q

Average Total Cost (ATC) = TC / Q = AFC + AVC

Average cost means cost per unit. As output rises, AFC usually falls because the same fixed cost is spread across more units.

9.4 Marginal cost

Marginal Cost (MC) = ΔTC / ΔQ

Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one additional unit. Since fixed cost does not change when output changes in the short run, marginal cost is also the change in variable cost divided by the change in output.

9.5 Opportunity cost and sunk cost

Concept

Meaning

Decision rule

Opportunity cost

Value of the best alternative given up when a resource is used.

Include it in economic decision-making.

Sunk cost

Past expenditure that has been made and cannot be recovered.

Do not let it determine a future decision.

Example from the slides: a firm owns its building and pays no rent. The economic cost of using the building is not zero because it could have rented the building out. The rent it gives up is an opportunity cost.

pages.title: Section 20
pages.text:
A non-refundable advance already paid for a building option is a sunk cost. If a better building becomes available, the firm should compare future costs and benefits rather than buy the first building merely because it has already paid the advance.

9.6 Costs in the short run

The lecture links marginal cost to marginal product of labour. If each extra worker adds a lot of output, the cost of producing an extra unit can be low. If each extra worker adds little output, marginal cost can be high.

Relationship Increasing marginal product of labour tends to reduce marginal cost. Decreasing marginal product of labour tends to increase marginal cost, assuming the wage rate is fixed.

9.7 Long-run cost and opportunity cost of capital

In the long run, firms can change capital and labour. The economic cost of capital includes depreciation and the return that could have been earned by investing the money elsewhere.

User cost of capital = Economic depreciation + (Interest rate × Value of capital)

The slides give an airplane example: purchase price $150 million, useful life 30 years, annual economic depreciation $5 million and interest rate 10%. In year 1, user cost is $5m + 10% × $150m = $20m.

9.8 Isocost line and cost-minimising input choice

An isocost line shows combinations of labour and capital that have the same total cost.

C = wL + rK

w is the wage rate, r is the price/rental rate of capital, L is labour and K is capital.

K = C/r − (w/r)L

The slope is −w/r. Combining an isocost line with an isoquant helps a firm find the lowest-cost input combination for a given output.

9.9 Short run versus long run costs

In the short run, some inputs are fixed, so the firm may not be able to produce at the lowest possible cost. In the long run, the firm can adjust plant size and capital, potentially lowering average cost for a given output.

9.10 Economies of scale, scope and learning curve

Concept

Meaning

Example

Economies of scale

pages.title: Section 21
pages.text:
Average cost falls as the scale/volume of production increases.

A larger factory spreads fixed costs and allows specialisation.

Diseconomies of scale

Average cost rises when the firm becomes too large or difficult to manage.

Coordination and management complexity.

Economies of scope

Producing two or more products together costs less than producing them separately.

A delivery network used for multiple product categories.

Learning curve

Unit cost falls as cumulative experience or output increases.

Workers become faster and processes improve with practice.

9.11 Estimating cost

The cost deck includes a cubic cost function example:

TC = 200 + 5Q − 0.04Q² + 0.001Q³

From a total cost function, fixed cost is the part that does not depend on Q. Variable cost is the part that changes with Q. Average cost is TC/Q, and marginal cost is the derivative of TC with respect to Q.

For the example: FC = 200; VC = 5Q − 0.04Q² + 0.001Q³

MC = dTC/dQ = 5 − 0.08Q + 0.003Q²

SESSION 10: Firm’s Decision in a Competitive Market

From the course outline: Profit maximisation, price-taking firms, marginal revenue and marginal cost, short-run output and shutdown, firm and industry supply, long-run equilibrium.

10.1 Firm objective and profit

The lecture assumes that a firm's objective is to maximise profit.

Profit (π) = Total Revenue (TR) − Total Cost (TC)

TR = P × Q

Total cost includes fixed and variable costs and, in economic analysis, opportunity costs.

10.2 Perfectly competitive market

A competitive market is one in which no single firm can influence the market price. A firm in this market is a price taker: it accepts the market price.

Many buyers and sellers.

Firms sell a homogeneous/standardised product.

pages.title: Section 22
pages.text:
Individual firms cannot influence the market price.

The lecture's competitive-market discussion includes free entry and exit.

10.3 Revenue for a competitive firm

Because the firm is a price taker, it can sell additional units at the market price, within the model.

Average Revenue (AR) = TR/Q = P

Marginal Revenue (MR) = ΔTR/ΔQ = P

Key result For a perfectly competitive firm: P = AR = MR. The firm's demand curve is a horizontal line at the market price.

10.4 Profit maximisation rule

Choose output where MR = MC, provided producing is better than shutting down.

If MR is greater than MC, producing one more unit adds more revenue than cost, so increasing output raises profit. If MC is greater than MR, the extra unit costs more than it earns, so reducing output raises profit. The profit-maximising point is where MR and MC meet on the relevant rising part of MC.

10.5 Short-run decisions

In the short run, at least one input is fixed. A firm can make a profit, incur a loss and still choose to produce if revenue covers variable costs and contributes something toward fixed costs.

Condition

Decision intuition

P > ATC

Firm earns positive economic profit.

P = ATC

Firm earns zero economic profit (normal return included in economic cost).

AVC < P < ATC

Firm incurs a loss but may continue producing because it covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.

P < AVC

Firm should shut down in the short run under the standard rule because revenue does not cover variable cost.

Short-run shutdown rule: produce if P ≥ minimum AVC; shut down if P < minimum AVC.

10.6 Short-run supply curve

The firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of its marginal cost curve above the minimum point of average variable cost. It shows how much the firm will produce at different market prices.

10.7 Market / industry supply

pages.title: Section 23
pages.text:
The short-run market supply curve is obtained by adding the quantities supplied by all firms horizontally at each price. When price rises, firms generally expand output along their supply curves.

10.8 Long-run competitive equilibrium

In the long run, firms can enter or leave the industry and adjust all inputs. If firms earn positive economic profits, new firms have an incentive to enter. Entry increases industry supply and puts downward pressure on price and profit. If firms incur economic losses, some firms may exit, reducing supply and putting upward pressure on price.

In the standard long-run competitive equilibrium described in the lecture, firms maximise profit and earn zero economic profit. Zero economic profit does not mean the owner receives no return; normal opportunity costs are included in economic cost.

10.9 Industry long-run supply

The shape of the industry's long-run supply curve depends on how industry expansion affects the prices firms pay for inputs. If input prices remain unchanged, industry supply may be relatively flat; if input prices rise, it may slope upward; if input prices fall, it may slope downward. The exact case depends on the industry.

Worked numerical example

Suppose a competitive firm faces market price P = ₹100 and has marginal cost MC = 0.002Q. Under competition, MR = P.

MR = MC → 100 = 0.002Q → Q = 50,000 units

This is the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, subject to the shutdown condition and the relevant cost curves.

Answer: Quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied, creating a shortage. This creates upward pressure on price.

MARKETING RESEARCH

Impact of Instagram Skincare Influencers on Gen Z Purchase Decisions in India

Assignment Submission

Submitted by: ______________________________Programme / Section: ________________________Course: Marketing ResearchSubmitted to: ______________________________Date: _____________________________________

Q1. Marketing Research Problem

1.1 Background

Instagram has become an important platform for skincare brands to reach young consumers. Brands increasingly collaborate with influencers to introduce products, share skincare routines and shape opinions. However, brands may not clearly know whether exposure to this content leads to purchase decisions, or which influencer qualities make consumers more likely to consider a product. This research focuses on Gen Z consumers in India and examines the relationship between Instagram skincare influencer content, consumer trust and purchase intention.

1.2 Management Decision Problem (MDP)

How should skincare brands in India use Instagram influencer marketing to increase purchase decisions among Gen Z consumers?

1.3 Marketing Research Problem (MRP)

To what extent do Instagram skincare influencers influence the purchase decisions of Gen Z consumers in India, and which influencer attributes (credibility, authenticity, relatability and content quality) have the greatest influence?

1.4 Difference between MDP and MRP

Management Decision Problem (MDP)

Marketing Research Problem (MRP)

Focuses on what management should do.

Focuses on what information research needs to provide.

Action-oriented and helps management make a business decision.

Information-oriented and helps understand the problem.

Example: How should the brand use influencer marketing?

Example: Which influencer attributes are associated with purchase intention?

1.5 Research Objectives

To measure how much skincare content from Instagram influencers Gen Z consumers are exposed to.

To identify which influencer attributes Gen Z consumers value most.

To examine the level of purchase intention among Gen Z consumers who follow skincare influencers.

To examine whether consumers who trust skincare influencers more report higher purchase intention.

To compare purchase intention across gender and city tier.

To suggest how skincare brands can select and work with influencers more effectively.

1.6 Research Questions

RQ1: How much are Gen Z consumers exposed to skincare content from Instagram influencers?

RQ2: Which influencer attributes do Gen Z consumers value most?

RQ3: Do consumers with higher trust in influencers have higher purchase intention?

RQ4: Does purchase intention differ by gender or city tier?

1.7 Hypotheses

H1: The average purchase-decision score of Gen Z consumers exposed to skincare influencers is significantly higher than the neutral score of 3.

H2: Consumers who follow more skincare influencers have significantly higher purchase intention than those who follow fewer influencers.

H3: Consumers with high trust in influencers have significantly higher purchase intention than consumers with low trust.

H4: Purchase intention differs significantly between male and female respondents.

H5: Purchase intention differs significantly across city tiers (metro, Tier 2 and Tier 3).

H6: There is a significant association between gender and the influencer attribute respondents value most.

Note: For formal hypothesis testing, each research hypothesis can be expressed as a null hypothesis (H0) and an alternative hypothesis (H1). In this document, H1–H6 are numbered research hypotheses.

1.8 Information Areas

Information area

What needs to be known

Respondent profile

Age, gender, city tier, education, pocket money or income.

Instagram usage

Time spent on Instagram, frequency of viewing skincare content and number of skincare influencers followed.

Skincare behaviour

Skin concerns, product types purchased, purchase frequency, spending and favourite brands.

Influencer attributes

Perceived expertise, credibility, trustworthiness, authenticity, relatability and content quality.

Trust

Trust in the influencer and trust in the brand or product being recommended.

Sponsorship awareness

Whether respondents notice paid-promotion disclosures and whether sponsorship affects their trust.

Purchase decision

Purchase intention, actual purchase after seeing influencer content, repeat purchase and recommendation to others.

Other influencing factors

Friends and family, dermatologists, online reviews, price, advertisements and product availability.

PART 2. Research Design (BLUEPRNT)

Overall research design: Quantitative, cross-sectional and descriptive-cum-comparative research using a structured online survey. The study will describe exposure and influencer preferences and compare purchase-intention scores across relevant respondent groups. Since the survey is observational and collects data at one point in time, it can identify associations and group differences but cannot establish that influencer exposure causes purchases.

2.1 BLUEPRNT Framework

Letter

Element

Design choice

Justification

B

Background & Purpose

Conclusive research, mainly descriptive with a comparative component.

The study describes exposure and preferences and examines differences in purchase intention across groups.

L

Logic of Time

Cross-sectional; data collected once.

It fits the academic timeline and allows comparison at one point in time. Results may vary with trends and sale seasons.

U

Unit of Analysis

Individual Gen Z consumer in India, approximately 18–27 years old.

Individuals make purchase decisions. Respondents should actively use Instagram, follow at least one skincare influencer and have bought or considered skincare products.

E

Evidence Type

Primary quantitative data, supported by secondary data.

Survey responses provide direct information about perceptions and intentions. Reports and previous studies provide background.

P

Procedure for Data Collection

Structured online questionnaire using Google Forms, with screening questions, demographics and a pilot test of 20–30 respondents.

Online collection is relatively quick and low-cost and can reach respondents through Instagram, WhatsApp and college networks.

R

Reach (Sampling)

Non-probability purposive sampling with a snowball extension. Proposed sample: 150–300 respondents.

There is no complete sampling list of Gen Z Instagram users. The approach is practical, but may involve self-selection bias and limited generalisability.

N

Numbers & Measurement

Five-point Likert scale: 1 = strongly disagree and 5 = strongly agree. Measure exposure, influencer attributes, trust and purchase intention.

The scale converts opinions into scores that can be summarised and compared. Demographics such as age, gender and city tier support group comparisons.

T

Techniques of Analysis

Descriptive statistics, one-sample and independent-samples t-tests, ANOVA and chi-square test, as appropriate.

The selected techniques match the type of variables and the research hypotheses.

2.2 Techniques of Analysis and Their Link to Objectives

Technique

Purpose

Objective / Hypothesis

Descriptive statistics (frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation and charts)

Profile respondents, measure exposure and compare average ratings of influencer attributes.

Objectives 1 and 2

One-sample t-test

Test whether the average purchase-intention score differs from the neutral value of 3.

Objective 3; H1

Independent-samples t-test

Compare purchase-intention scores between two groups, such as higher vs lower influencer following, high vs low trust, or male vs female respondents.

Objectives 4 and 5; H2, H3 and H4

One-way ANOVA

Compare average purchase-intention scores across three city-tier groups.

Objective 5; H5

Chi-square test of independence

Check whether gender is associated with the categorical influencer attribute selected as most important.

H6

2.3 Notes on Statistical Testing

A one-sample t-test is generally suitable for testing whether a sample mean differs from a reference value when the population standard deviation is unknown. A one-sample z-test is appropriate when the population standard deviation is known and the assumptions are met.

An independent-samples t-test can compare the means of two independent groups. The groups and cut-off used to define 'more' versus 'fewer' influencers, or 'high' versus 'low' trust, should be decided before analysis.

ANOVA is suitable for comparing mean purchase-intention scores across three or more independent groups, such as metro, Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities.

The chi-square test is suitable when both variables are categorical, such as gender and the single influencer attribute selected as most important.

The researcher should check relevant assumptions, data quality and sample sizes before selecting a test. Statistical significance does not by itself prove causation.

2.4 Scope and Limitations

The study is limited to Gen Z Instagram users in India who meet the screening criteria. The use of purposive and snowball sampling means the sample may not represent all Gen Z consumers. Responses are self-reported and may be affected by recall errors or socially desirable answers. Because the study is cross-sectional and observational, it can show relationships between influencer attributes, trust and purchase intention, but it cannot prove that influencer content directly causes a purchase. Actual purchase behaviour may also be influenced by price, product quality, skin needs, recommendations from dermatologists, friends and family, and product availability.

Conclusion

This research will help understand how Instagram skincare influencers are connected with Gen Z consumers' purchase intention in India. By examining exposure, credibility, authenticity, relatability, content quality and trust, the study aims to identify the influencer attributes that consumers value. The findings can provide useful information to skincare brands when planning their influencer-marketing activities and selecting suitable creators.

options: The company is overspending on marketing and will soon become insolvent.

steps.description: Define the smallest functional product that delivers the core value proposition without building superfluous features.
steps.metrics: Development time < 6 weeks, Core feature set < 3 items
steps.example: Dropbox released a simple 3-minute demo video before writing production cloud sync code.

steps.description: Launch to a targeted cohort. Track acquisition cost (CAC), activation rate, and early customer feedback.
steps.metrics: CAC / LTV ratio > 3x, Retention cohort curve flattens
steps.example: Testing ad conversion on Google search ads to validate willingness to pay.

steps.title: 4. Scale, Distribution & Optimization
steps.description: Automate sales funnels, optimize margins, and build defensive moats (network effects, switching costs).
steps.example: Expanding distribution through organic referral loops and strategic B2B partnerships.

stages.title: Stable Equilibrium
stages.description: At $50, quantity demanded (100 units) matches quantity supplied (100 units). Market clears without surplus or shortage.

stages.title: Supply Shock (Raw Material Shortage)
stages.description: Supply curve shifts left. At old price $50, there is a shortage. Price bids up to $70, reducing demand to 75 units.

stages.title: Demand Surge (Viral Trend / Subsidy)
stages.description: Demand curve shifts right as consumer preference increases. Equilibrium price rises to $85 and output expands to 110 units.

visualStudioItems.explanation: Explore how supply and demand curves shift when market conditions change, and observe how price and quantity adjust toward equilibrium.
